steps.title: Split down to single items
steps.caption: Halve the array, then halve the halves, down to single items: no comparisons yet.
steps.body: The array is cut in half at `mid = (lo + hi) // 2`, each half is cut again, and so on until every piece holds one item. Splitting is only index arithmetic, so the counter stays at 0, and a piece of one item is already sorted. Halving 8 items down to 1 takes three rounds: log₂ 8 = 3.

steps.title: Merge back up
steps.caption: Merge neighbours into sorted pairs, then pairs into sorted fours: 10 comparisons so far.
steps.body: A merge of two sorted runs only ever compares their front items, the **heads**, and moves the smaller one up. Level 1 merges single items into four sorted pairs with one comparison each; level 2 merges the pairs into [2 4 5 7] and [1 2 3 6] with three comparisons each. The counter reaches 10.

steps.title: One merge, close up
steps.caption: The smaller head moves up each time; on the 2a = 2b tie the left one goes first, so it is stable.
steps.body: In the final merge `i` and `j` point at the heads of the two sorted halves, and each comparison sends the smaller head to the next free slot of the output. On the tie between 2a and 2b the left one goes first, so equal keys keep their input order: that is what makes merge sort **stable**. Seven comparisons bring the counter to 17; when the right half runs out, the 7 is copied over without one.

steps.title: Always n log n
steps.caption: 3 levels of 8 moves each: 24 for any input, so the worst case stays O(n log n). Cost: n extra cells.
steps.body: Halving 8 items takes log₂ 8 = 3 levels, and each level of merging moves all 8 items once: 24 moves whatever the input order, with 12 to 17 comparisons (this input needs the most). So the worst case stays **O(n log n)**, where quicksort's can degrade to O(n²). The price is a buffer of n extra cells for the merges; Timsort, a merge sort hybrid, is the stable sort behind Python's `sorted()`, Java's object sorts and V8's `Array.prototype.sort`.
